question: Which of the following best describes a wave on a spring?
options: A disturbance that moves through the spring while each part of the spring oscillates about a fixed position
The net flow of spring material from one end to the other
A transfer of matter accompanied by the disturbance
A stationary pattern with no energy transfer
explanation: When a spring is jerk/squeezed at one end, the disturbance travels along it but each coil merely oscillates about its mean position — a wave is a pattern moving without the physical flow of matter as a whole. The jumping ball on traveling bobbing waves (bobbing corks in a pond) shows the same idea: energy moves, matter stays.

question: Which of the following types of waves requires a material medium for propagation?
options: Mechanical waves (string, water, sound, seismic)
Electromagnetic waves, which travel at c = 299,792,458 m s⁻¹ in vacuum
Gravitational waves
Matter waves associated with free electrons
explanation: Mechanical waves need a medium (their constituents oscillate and elastic properties restore them); they cannot pass through a vacuum. Electromagnetic waves need no medium and in vacuum all travel at the speed of light. Matter waves accompany electrons/protons/atoms (quantum) and are used, e.g., in electron microscopes.

question: In a transverse wave, the constituents of the medium:
options: Oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation
Oscillate along the direction of propagation
Move as a whole with the wave speed
Oscillate only in circles
explanation: A transverse wave is one in which the particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation — e.g. an up-down jerk on a string sends a pulse travelling right while each element moves up/down. A longitudinal wave, in contrast, has constituents oscillating along the direction of propagation (piston pushing air).

question: A longitudinal wave travelling through a fluid consists of:
options: Condensations (higher density) and rarefactions (lower density) alternating along the direction of propagation
Nodes and antinodes fixed in space
Particles moving perpendicular to the wave direction
A uniform density with no pressure change
explanation: A piston pushed forward/backward in a pipe filled with air sends a pulse made of condensations and rarefactions — regions of higher and lower density. The change in density δρ leads to a pressure change δp which provides the restoring force; particles oscillate along the direction of propagation.

question: Transverse waves can travel through:
options: Only media that can sustain shearing stress — solids (not fluids)
All elastic media including gases
Only liquids and gases
The vacuum
explanation: Transverse waves require shearing stress between layers, so only media that sustain shear — solids — support them; fluids support no static shear. Longitudinal waves need bulk (compressive) strain, so they travel in all elastic media — solids, liquids and gases. Steel supports both; air only longitudinal. Water surface waves involve a combination of up-down and back-forth motion.

question: Sound waves produced by a quartz crystal in air (ultrasonic) are:
options: Longitudinal waves
Transverse waves
Electromagnetic waves
Matter waves
explanation: Air sustains volume (bulk) changes but not shear, so any wave supported by air is longitudinal. A quartz crystal in air produces longitudinal ultrasonic waves; the same quartz oscillating in water also produces longitudinal waves. (Example 14.1.)

question: For the progressive wave y(x,t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ), the phase (kx − ωt + φ):
options: Is constant along a point moving with the wave speed, so the wave travels along +x
Travels along −x with the negative sign in front of ωt
Is fixed in space for all time
Equals the amplitude a
explanation: To keep kx − ωt + φ constant as time increases, x must increase — so the wave travels along the +x direction. The alternative form y = a sin(kx + ωt + φ) travels along −x. Fixing t gives the wave shape in space; fixing x gives SHM of the element in time.

question: Which of the following functions represents a wave travelling along the negative x-axis?
options: y(x,t) = a sin(kx + ωt + φ)
y(x,t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ)
y(x,t) = a cos(kx − ωt)
y(x,t) = a sin kx cos ωt
explanation: Keeping kx + ωt + φ constant requires x to decrease as t grows, i.e. propagation along −x (Eq 14.4). The form kx − ωt travels along +x, and y = a sin kx cos ωt is a standing wave. The sine/cosine choice is irrelevant; the sign between the x and t terms decides the direction.

question: The amplitude a of a progressive wave is:
options: The maximum displacement of the medium's particles, a positive constant
The distance between two consecutive crests
The time for one full oscillation
The number of waves per unit length
explanation: The displacement y of a transverse wave y = a sin(kx − ωt + φ) varies between +a and −a; a is the amplitude — the magnitude of maximum displacement, taken as a positive constant. Crests are maxima of y and troughs minima.

question: The wavelength λ of a wave is:
options: The minimum distance between two points having the same phase (e.g. consecutive crests)
The distance the wave travels in one second
The maximum displacement of a particle
One-quarter of the distance between a node and its adjacent antinode
explanation: λ is the minimum distance between points in the same phase — for example between consecutive crests or troughs. With φ = 0 at t = 0 the wave shape is y = a sin kx; since sin θ repeats after 2π, the wavelength corresponds to kλ = 2π, giving λ = 2π/k.

question: The angular wave number k and wavelength λ are related by:
options: k = 2π/λ, with SI unit rad m⁻¹
k = λ/2π
k = 1/λ
k = 2πλ
explanation: Because sin θ repeats after a phase change of 2π, kλ = 2π so λ = 2π/k (Eq 14.6) and k = 2π/λ. k is the angular wave number quoted in radians per metre (radians being dimensionless, it is often written simply as m⁻¹); it equals 2π times the number of complete waves per unit length.

question: The angular frequency ω and the period T of a wave are related by:
options: ω = 2π/T, SI unit rad s⁻¹
ω = T/2π, SI unit s
ω = 2πT, SI unit s⁻¹
ω = 1/T, SI unit Hz
explanation: An element of the medium undergoes one full oscillation in time T; its phase changes by 2π in that time, so ωT = 2π, giving ω = 2π/T (Eq 14.7) with SI unit rad s⁻¹. The frequency ν = 1/T = ω/2π is measured in hertz (Hz).

question: The speed of a travelling wave is given by:
options: v = ω/k = λν = λ/T
v = kω
v = k/ω
v = 1/λν
explanation: A point of constant phase satisfies kx − ωt = constant; differentiating gives v = dx/dt = ω/k (Eq 14.11). Since ω = 2πν and k = 2π/λ, this equals λν = λ/T (Eq 14.12) — in one period the wave pattern advances by one wavelength.

question: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string of tension T and linear mass density μ is:
options: v = √(T/μ) — fixed by the medium properties, independent of frequency
v = νλ, which depends only on the source frequency
v = Tμ
explanation: The restoring force is the tension T and the inertial property is the linear mass density μ. Dimensionally T/μ has units L²T⁻², so v = √(T/μ) (Eq 14.14). Given v, the source frequency fixes the wavelength via λ = v/ν (Eq 14.15); different frequencies of the same string give different λ but the same speed.

question: A steel wire 0.72 m long with mass 5.0 × 10⁻³ kg is under a tension of 60 N. The speed of a transverse wave on it is:
options: v = √(T/μ) with μ = 6.9 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹, giving about 93 m s⁻¹
v = √(μ/T), giving about 0.01 m s⁻¹
v = T/μ, giving about 8700 m s⁻¹
v = (Tμ), giving about 0.41 m s⁻¹
explanation: μ = m/L = 5.0 × 10⁻³ / 0.72 = 6.9 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹. Then v = √(T/μ) = √(60 / 6.9 × 10⁻³) ≈ 93 m s⁻¹. Using v = √(T/μ) with the correct exponent on μ is the key step. (Example 14.3.)

question: The speed of a longitudinal wave in a fluid of bulk modulus B and density ρ is:
options: v = B/ρ
v = √(Bρ)
explanation: The restoring force comes from the bulk modulus B = −ΔP/(ΔV/V), and the inertial property is the density ρ. Their ratio B/ρ has the dimensions of velocity squared, so v = √(B/ρ) (Eq 14.19). For a longitudinal wave in a long solid bar, B is replaced by Young's modulus Y: v = √(Y/ρ). Liquids and solids have higher sound speeds than gases because their larger bulk modulus outweighs their higher density.

question: Newton's formula for the speed of sound in a gas (v = √(P/ρ)) predicted about 280 m s⁻¹ at STP, ~15% below the measured 331 m s⁻¹, because:
options: It assumed isothermal pressure variations; Laplace corrected it to adiabatic v = √(γP/ρ) with γ = 7/5 for air, giving 331.3 m s⁻¹
It assumed the wrong value of the gas constant R
Sound in air is transverse, not longitudinal
It ignored the density of air
explanation: Newton assumed the compressions/rarefactions occur without heat exchange with the surroundings i.e., isothermally, so B = P. Laplace noted the pressure variations are too fast for heat flow — the change is adiabatic, PV^γ = constant, giving B = γP, hence v = √(γP/ρ) (Eq 14.24). For air γ = 7/5 this gives 331.3 m s⁻¹, matching measurement.

question: The principle of superposition of waves states that:
options: The resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements: y = y₁ + y₂
The amplitudes always add in magnitude
Waves lose their identity permanently after meeting
The speed of a wave is the sum of the speeds of its components
explanation: When two pulses meet, the displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the displacements the waves would produce separately: y(x,t) = y₁(x,t) + y₂(x,t) (Eq 14.25). After crossing, the pulses emerge with their shapes unaltered — the waves superpose (add) in the region of overlap only. This is the basis of interference.

question: Two identical waves (same a, ω, k) travelling along +x with a phase difference of π interfere. The result is:
options: y = 0 everywhere — total destructive interference
Doubled amplitude 2a — constructive interference
Beats at the difference frequency
A standing wave with nodes and antinodes
explanation: For two equal-amplitude waves with phase difference φ, the resultant is y = 2a cos(φ/2) sin(kx − ωt + φ/2) (Eq 14.31) with amplitude A = 2a cos(φ/2). At φ = 0, A = 2a (constructive, Eq 14.33); at φ = π, cos(π/2) = 0 so y = 0 everywhere — destructive interference (Eq 14.34).

question: When a pulse reflects from a RIGID boundary (e.g. a string fixed at a wall), it:
options: Returns with the same shape but a phase change of π, so the displacement at the boundary is zero
Returns unchanged with no phase change
Is absorbed completely at the wall
Doubles its amplitude
explanation: At a rigid boundary the reflected pulse has the same shape but the phase is reversed (a phase change of π): y_r = a sin(kx − ωt + π) = −a sin(kx − ωt) (Eq 14.35). The boundary displacement y + y_r = 0 at all times — the rigid end is a node, as with a sound echo bouncing off a wall.

question: Reflection from a NON-rigid or OPEN boundary (a string tied to a freely moving ring, or the open end of a pipe):
options: Occurs with NO phase change, so the boundary displacement reaches twice the amplitude
Occurs with a phase change of π, giving a node at the boundary
Is impossible — open ends do not reflect
Converts the wave to longitudinal
explanation: At a non-rigid/open boundary the force from the boundary vanishes, so the reflected wave has no phase change: y_r = a sin(kx − ωt) (Eq 14.36). Incident and reflected waves add to give a maximum displacement of 2a at the boundary. Physically this is what happens at the open end of an organ pipe.

question: A standing wave y = 2a sin kx cos ωt on a string has:
options: Nodes at x = nλ/2 and antinodes at x = (n + ½)λ/2, separated by λ/2
Nodes spaced half a wavelength at x = nλ
Antinodes fixed at x = nλ/2
Amplitude 2a everywhere with no fixed nodes
explanation: Two equal waves travelling in opposite directions superpose to give y = 2a sin kx cos ωt (Eq 14.37). The amplitude 2a sin kx varies point to point: nodes (amplitude 0) where sin kx = 0, i.e. x = nλ/2 (Eq 14.38); antinodes (amplitude maximum) where |sin kx| = 1, i.e. x = (n + ½)λ/2 (Eq 14.39). Node–node or antinode–antinode spacing is λ/2.

question: For a string of length L fixed at both ends, the allowed standing-wave frequencies are:
options: ν = nv/2L for n = 1, 2, 3, … (fundamental v/2L)
ν = (2n + 1)v/4L — odd harmonics only
ν = nv/4L
ν = v/2L only — a single frequency
explanation: The fixed ends are nodes, so the string must fit n half-wavelengths: L = nλ/2 (Eq 14.41), giving λ = 2L/n and ν = nv/2L (Eq 14.42), n = 1, 2, 3, … The n = 1 mode is the fundamental (first harmonic), n = 2 the second harmonic, and so on. Where and how the string is plucked decides which harmonics dominate.

question: A pipe closed at one end (antinode at the open end, node at the closed end) supports:
options: Only ODD harmonics: ν = (2n + 1)v/4L, with fundamental v/4L
All harmonics ν = nv/2L like an open pipe
No standing waves at all
Only even harmonics
explanation: For a column of length L closed at one end, L = (n + ½)λ/2 (Eq 14.43) so ν = (2n + 1)v/4L (Eq 14.44), n = 0, 1, 2, … — the fundamental is v/4L and only the odd harmonics v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L appear. An open pipe (two antinode ends) allows all harmonics nv/2L. Both are examples of normal modes; forced oscillation at a natural frequency produces resonance.

question: When two waves of close (not equal) frequencies, e.g. 11 Hz and 9 Hz, travel together, the listener hears:
options: Beats — the intensity waxes and wanes at the difference frequency ν₁ − ν₂ = 2 Hz
Only the lower 9 Hz tone
A single tone of 20 Hz
No sound at all
explanation: Superposing s₁ = a cos ω₁t and s₂ = a cos ω₂t gives s = 2a cos(ω_b t) cos(ω_a t) with ω_b = (ω₁ − ω₂)/2 and ω_a = (ω₁ + ω₂)/2 (Eq 14.46, 14.47). The wave oscillates at the average frequency while its amplitude waxes and wanes at the beat frequency ν_b = ν₁ − ν₂ (Eq 14.48). Musicians tune instruments by listening for beats.

question: The beat frequency produced by two tuning forks of frequencies ν₁ and ν₂ is:
options: ν₁ − ν₂
ν₁ + ν₂
(ν₁ + ν₂)/2
(ν₁ − ν₂)/2
explanation: The amplitude of the combined wave modulates at twice ω_b, i.e. at the difference of the angular frequencies, so the beat frequency is ν_b = |ν₁ − ν₂| (Eq 14.48). Two forks of 427 Hz and 422 Hz produce 5 beats per second.

question: A sitar string A vibrates at 427 Hz and produces 5 beats per second with another string B. When the tension of B is increased, the beat frequency drops to 3 Hz. The frequency of B is:
options: 422 Hz — increase tension would raise beats if ν_B > ν_A
432 Hz
430 Hz
424 Hz
explanation: Increasing tension raises the frequency of B. If ν_B were above A, raising it would increase the beat frequency — but the beats fell, so ν_B < ν_A: ν_B = 427 − 5 = 422 Hz. (Example 14.6.)

question: A transverse wave on a string is described by y = 0.005 sin(80.0x − 3.0t) in SI units. Determine (i) the amplitude, (ii) the wavelength, (iii) the period, and (iv) the frequency of the wave.
answer: Compare with y = a sin(kx − ωt): (i) a = 0.005 m = 5 mm. (ii) k = 80.0 m⁻¹, so λ = 2π/k = 2π/80.0 = 7.85 cm. (iii) ω = 3.0 s⁻¹, so T = 2π/ω = 2π/3.0 = 2.09 s. (iv) ν = 1/T = 0.48 Hz. Answers: (i) 5 mm, (ii) 7.85 cm, (iii) 2.09 s, (iv) 0.48 Hz.
explanation: The general form is y = a sin(kx − ωt + φ); here φ = 0. Read a, k and ω straight from the equation, then use λ = 2π/k and T = 2π/ω. For example, at x = 30.0 cm and t = 20 s the displacement is y = 0.005 sin(−36 + 12π) = 0.005 sin(1.699) ≈ 5 mm. (Example 14.2.)

question: A steel wire has a mass of 2.50 kg and is stretched between two supports 20.0 m apart under a tension of 200 N. If a transverse jerk is struck at one end, how long does the pulse take to reach the other end?
explanation: The transverse wave speed depends only on the medium: v = √(T/μ). Converting the mass to a linear mass density and finding the speed, then dividing the distance by the speed, gives the travel time — the pulse does not carry the wire with it, it simply propagates along it. (Exercise 14.1.)

question: A pipe 20 cm long is closed at one end. A tuning fork of 430 Hz is held near its open end. Given v = 340 m s⁻¹, (i) which harmonic of the closed pipe is set into resonance, and (ii) would the pipe resonate at any frequency if both ends were open?
answer: (i) Closed-pipe fundamental ν₁ = v/4L = 340/(4 × 0.20) = 425 Hz. The fork at 430 Hz is closest to this fundamental, so the pipe resonates in the fundamental mode (a closed pipe supports only odd harmonics (2n − 1)v/4L; 430 ≈ 425 is the n = 1 fundamental). (ii) If both ends were open the allowed frequencies are ν = nv/2L = n × 850 Hz (n = 1, 2, 3, …); 430 Hz is not a multiple of 850 Hz, so no resonance would occur. Answers: (i) fundamental (first mode) of the closed pipe; (ii) no resonance for the open pipe.
explanation: A pipe closed at one end has its fundamental at v/4L and only odd harmonics; a pipe open at both ends has all harmonics nv/2L. The integer m = 2Lν/v = 2 × 0.20 × 430/340 = 0.505 is not even close to an integer, confirming the open pipe cannot resonate with 430 Hz. (Exercise 14.17.)
